task.objective: Use a fixed population and two deduplicated attendance counts to justify feasible attendance bounds with concrete allocations.

inputs.text: record-1: Fictional seed-club register: Cedar Exchange had twenty-eight registered members throughout April. The register did not change, and both April workshops admitted only these registered members.

record-2: The sowing workshop recorded nineteen distinct members. The storage workshop recorded seventeen distinct members. Each attendance list counted a member once, regardless of how long they stayed.
record-3: The two attendance lists have not been matched to identify members attending both. Visiting members of other clubs were not admitted to either workshop.

task.title: Bound participation when memberships overlap
task.product: One set diagram or four-group table, bounds with calculations, and a statement of missing evidence.
task.question: For “Cedar Exchange”, give every possible integer count of members attending at least one of “sowing workshop” and “storage workshop”, and every possible integer count attending both. Explain how the two counts are paired. Derive the sharp bounds, construct both endpoint allocations, justify all intermediate counts, and state whether the union proportion is exact and what further membership evidence would determine it.
directions: Label the roster and both event sets.
Construct and check both endpoint allocations.
Show that every intermediate integer count has a feasible four-group allocation.
Separate proven bounds from missing observations.
studentChecks: My four groups reproduce each count.
I did not assume independence or zero overlap.
task.summary: The intersection ranges from 8 to 17 members, including every integer. The attainable union ranges from 19 to 28 members: 19/28 ≈ 67.86% to 28/28 = 100%. An exact value is not determined.
task.answer:
“Cedar Exchange”: 28 members; “sowing workshop”: 19; “storage workshop”: 17. Common population: “Cedar Exchange had twenty-eight registered members throughout April. The register did not change, and both April workshops admitted only these registered members.” Within-event counting: “Each attendance list counted a member once, regardless of how long they stayed.”

Let x count members in both events. The union is 19 + 17 − x = 36 − x. Since x cannot exceed either event and the union cannot exceed 28, 8 ≤ x ≤ 17.

Minimum union: 19, giving 19/28 ≈ 67.86%. A feasible allocation is only “sowing workshop”: 2; only “storage workshop”: 0; both: 17; neither: 9. These nonnegative groups sum to 28 and reproduce both event counts.

Maximum union: 28, giving 28/28 = 100%. A feasible allocation is only “sowing workshop”: 11; only “storage workshop”: 9; both: 8; neither: 0. These nonnegative groups sum to 28 and reproduce both event counts.

Every integer x from 8 through 17 is possible. For any such x, assign 19 − x to only “sowing workshop”, 17 − x to only “storage workshop”, x to both, and 28 − (36 − x) to neither. All four counts are nonnegative integers, sum to 28, and reproduce 19 and 17. Thus the paired union count 36 − x takes every integer from 19 through 28; the two counts cannot be chosen independently.

The intersection ranges from 8 to 17 members, including every integer. The attainable union ranges from 19 to 28 members: 19/28 ≈ 67.86% to 28/28 = 100%. An exact value is not determined.

The record states: “The two attendance lists have not been matched to identify members attending both.” Missing does not mean zero or independent attendance. Match the two membership lists to establish x; then use (36 − x)/28. These conclusions apply only to the stable named population, not visits or people outside it.
